name: Roman religion
areas: the state cults of the city and its Latin neighbours
Italian cults drawn into Rome's; temples vowed in the Punic Wars
divine honours to Roman magnates, later the Imperial cult
the Imperial cult, developed first in the eastern provinces
Romanised cults, as at Vertault and Lugdunum
the Capitolium of Sabratha and the forum of Cuicul
soldiers' altars; around 250 binding spells found
routes: The Venus of Eryx brought from Sicily to the Capitoline (217 BCE)
The Magna Mater brought from Pessinus (206 BCE)
The Imperial cult takes root first in the eastern provinces
and then in the West, by the end of Augustus's reign
Aurelian establishes the cult of the Palmyrene Sol Invictus in Rome (270–275)
marks: The temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, founded in legend by Tarquinius Priscus, was the model for the highest official cult of the Roman world.
The Venus of Eryx was brought from here to a temple on the Capitoline hill in 217 BCE.
On the advice of the Sibylline books the Magna Mater was brought from here in 206 BCE; she was installed on the Palatine in 191 BCE.
The newly municipal town built a Capitolium near its temple to Liber Pater and Serapis; by the end of the 1st century CE its tophet was no longer in use.
All the known statues from its 2nd-century CE forum are of emperors or Concordia.
Theodosius I extinguished the Vestals' sacred fire and vacated their temple, ending official support for the old cults.
notes: The Republic begins (509 BCE); its elected magistrates also serve as priests, and its religion is held to go back to the kings, above all Numa.
During the Punic Wars (264–146 BCE) generals vow new temples, and Rome brings in the Venus of Eryx (217 BCE) and the Magna Mater of Pessinus (206 BCE).
From at least 195 BCE Roman magnates receive divine honours in the Greek East; in 186 BCE the Senate restricts the Bacchanals.
Julius Caesar becomes pontifex maximus (63 BCE), as priestly and political offices draw ever closer together.
Augustus revives and reforms the state cults; the Imperial cult grows first in the eastern provinces, then in the West.
Across the empire Roman and local gods are worshipped side by side, and traders and soldiers bring the cults of Cybele, Isis, Mithras and Sol Invictus.
Diocletian's edicts against the Christians (303–304) order churches and Christian texts destroyed, then universal sacrifice to the traditional gods.
The Edict of Milan (313) proclaims mutual toleration, and Constantine I funds the building of churches.
Under Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity becomes the state religion of the Roman Empire (380).
Theodosius I ends official support for all other cults and puts out the sacred fire of the Vestals (391).
src: Mary Beard, John North and Simon Price, Religions of Rome
